title: Question 1.1
statement_text: For which subsets $K \subset E^n$ does every red/blue-coloring of $E^n$ contain a red pair of points of distance one or a blue isometric copy of $K$?
context_text:
$\mathbb{E}^n$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean distance, $\ell_m$ is a sequence of $m$ points on a line with consecutive points at distance one (so $\ell_2$ is a pair of points at distance one), and a copy of a set always means an isometric copy. For sets $X,K$, $\mathbb{E}^n	o(X,K)$ means that every red/blue-coloring of $\mathbb{E}^n$ contains a red copy of $X$ or a blue copy of $K$, and $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(X,K)$ means that some red/blue-coloring contains neither. A set is $t$-separated if any two of its points are at distance at least $t$; logarithms are base 2. In this notation the question asks for which $K\subset\mathbb{E}^n$ one has $\mathbb{E}^n	o(\ell_2,K)$; it was studied by Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus. Known results: $\mathbb{E}^2	o(\ell_2,K)$ for every 3-point and (Juhász) every 4-point set $K$, $\mathbb{E}^2	o(\ell_2,\ell_5)$ (Tsaturian), $\mathbb{E}^3	o(\ell_2,K)$ for every 5-point $K$ (Iván) and $\mathbb{E}^3	o(\ell_2,\ell_6)$ (Arman and Tsaturian), while Csizmadia and Tóth found an 8-point planar $K$ (a regular heptagon with its center) with $\mathbb{E}^2
ot	o(\ell_2,K)$. Any subset $K$ of the unit sphere satisfies $\mathbb{E}^n	o(\ell_2,K)$, so $|K|$ can be unbounded. The authors prove that if $R>2$ and $K\subset\mathbb{E}^n$ is $1$-separated with diameter at most $R-1$ and $|K|>10^{4n}\log R$, then $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(\ell_2,K)$; in particular $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(\ell_2,\ell_m)$ for $m=10^{5n}$, answering a question of Erdős et al. The exponential size is necessary: by Szlam (via Frankl–Wilson), $\mathbb{E}^n	o(\ell_2,K)$ for every $K$ with $|K|\le 2^{c'n}$.
notes: The theorem header carries no parenthetical attribution; the paper notes it follows Erdős et al. [4] in studying this general question.

title: Erdős–Graham–Montgomery–Rothschild–Spencer–Straus Question on $\ell_2$ vs large sets
statement_text: For every natural number $n$, is there a set $K \subset E^1$ and a red/blue-coloring of $E^n$ containing no red copy of $\ell_2$ and no blue copy of $K$? More generally, for every natural number $d$, is there a natural number $n$ depending only on $d$ such that $E^n \not\to (\ell_2, K)$ for every $K \subset E^d$?
context_text: Erdős et al. stressed the case $d = 1$ and stated they expected the answer to be negative. The present paper's main theorem, Theorem 1.1, shows that for $m = 10^5 n$ one has $E^n \not\to (\ell_2, \ell_m)$, answering the question affirmatively and showing $n$ must grow logarithmically in $|K|$.
attributed_to: Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus
paper_contribution: Answers the question affirmatively for $d = 1$: for $m = 10^5 n$ there is a red/blue-coloring of $E^n$ with no red copy of $\ell_2$ and no blue copy of $\ell_m$, contradicting the authors' expectation.
notes: PDF source — question referenced in both the abstract and Section 1; attributed to [3] (1973) and [4] (1975) in the text.

title: Open problem: $E^n \not\to (\ell_3, \ell_m)$ for large $m$
statement_text: For every natural number $m$, does there exist a natural number $n$ such that $\mathbb{E}^n \to (\ell_3, \ell_m)$?
context_text:
$\mathbb{E}^n$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean distance, $\ell_m$ is a sequence of $m$ points on a line with consecutive points at distance one (so $\ell_2$ is a pair of points at distance one), and a copy of a set always means an isometric copy. For sets $X,K$, $\mathbb{E}^n	o(X,K)$ means that every red/blue-coloring of $\mathbb{E}^n$ contains a red copy of $X$ or a blue copy of $K$, and $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(X,K)$ means that some red/blue-coloring contains neither. A set is $t$-separated if any two of its points are at distance at least $t$; logarithms are base 2. A finite set $X$ is Ramsey if for every $r$ there is $n$ such that every $r$-coloring of $\mathbb{E}^n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $X$. The authors show that for every Ramsey set $X$ and finite $K$ there is $n$ with $\mathbb{E}^n	o(X,K)$, and conversely (assuming the axiom of choice) if a finite $X$ is not Ramsey then there is a finite set $K$ with $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(X,K)$ for all $n$. Being more particular about the choice of $K$, they were unable to decide this question for $X=\ell_3$ and $K=\ell_m$. They think it unlikely to hold for large $m$ (i.e. they suspect that for large $m$ one has $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(\ell_3,\ell_m)$ for all $n$) but could not exhibit a coloring confirming this. A first step was made by Erdős et al., who showed that $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(\ell_6,\ell_6)$ for all $n$.
notes: PDF source — stated in prose in the concluding remarks without a labelled theorem environment.

title: Erdős–Graham–Montgomery–Rothschild–Spencer–Straus Problem on universal two-coloring bound
statement_text: For every natural number $n$, does there exist a natural number $m$ depending only on $n$ such that for every set $K \subset E^n$ of size $m$ there is a two-coloring of $E^n$ with no monochromatic copy of $K$?
context_text: This problem from Erdős et al. [4] asks whether a universal size threshold $m(n)$ exists guaranteeing a monochromatic-free two-coloring for all point sets of that size in $E^n$. By rescaling one may assume $K$ is $1$-separated, so $\ell_2 \subset K$. Theorem 1.1 gives a partial answer when the diameter of $K$ is bounded.
attributed_to: Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus
paper_contribution: Partially answers the problem: if the diameter of $K \subset E^n$ is at most $R$ and $|K| > 10^4 n \log R$, then a two-coloring of $E^n$ with no monochromatic copy of $K$ exists; a complete answer requires removing the dependence on the diameter $R$.
notes: PDF source — stated in concluding remarks and attributed to [4].

title: Open problem: removing diameter dependence from Theorem 1.1
statement_text: The authors prove that if $R>2$ and $K\subset\mathbb{E}^n$ is a $1$-separated set of diameter at most $R-1$ with $|K|>10^{4n}\log R$, then $\mathbb{E}^n\not\to(\ell_2,K)$. Can the dependence on the diameter $R$ be removed from this result? That is, does there exist a function $f(n)$, independent of the diameter of $K$, such that $\mathbb{E}^n \not\to (\ell_2, K)$ for every $1$-separated set $K \subset \mathbb{E}^n$ with $|K| > f(n)$?
context_text: $\mathbb{E}^n$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean distance, $\ell_m$ is a sequence of $m$ points on a line with consecutive points at distance one (so $\ell_2$ is a pair of points at distance one), and a copy of a set always means an isometric copy. For sets $X,K$, $\mathbb{E}^n\to(X,K)$ means that every red/blue-coloring of $\mathbb{E}^n$ contains a red copy of $X$ or a blue copy of $K$, and $\mathbb{E}^n\not\to(X,K)$ means that some red/blue-coloring contains neither. A set is $t$-separated if any two of its points are at distance at least $t$; logarithms are base 2. Erdős et al. asked whether for every $n$ there is $m=m(n)$ such that for every set $K\subset\mathbb{E}^n$ of size $m$ there is a two-coloring of $\mathbb{E}^n$ with no monochromatic copy of $K$. Rescaling so that the smallest distance in $K$ is one, $K$ contains a copy of $\ell_2$ and is $1$-separated, so the authors' theorem (with its dependence on the diameter) gives a partial answer, and removing the dependence on $R$ would answer that question completely; the authors also find the problem interesting in its own right. The exponential dependence on $n$ is necessary, since $\mathbb{E}^n\to(\ell_2,K)$ for every $K$ of size at most $2^{c'n}$.
notes: PDF source — stated in prose in the concluding remarks without a labelled theorem environment.
